questions.q: What does `@njit` (as opposed to plain `@jit`) guarantee about how a function is compiled?
options: It guarantees the function will run on a GPU
It compiles in nopython mode, with no silent fallback to slow Python object representation
It guarantees the function will be parallelized automatically
It converts the function into a pandas UDF
questions.explain: `@njit` is shorthand for `jit(nopython=True)`, forcing full compilation with no object-mode fallback -- the mode needed to actually get Numba's speed benefit.

questions.q: In the measured example, the first call to a `@njit` function took 332.19 ms while the second call took 0.0136 ms. Why?
options: The second call used a smaller input
The first call paid the one-time cost of compiling the function for that argument type; subsequent calls reuse the cached compiled version
Numba caches results, not compiled code, so the second call just looked up a stored answer
The machine was under less load during the second call
questions.explain: Numba compiles lazily on first call with a given set of argument types and caches the compiled machine code; later calls with the same argument types skip compilation entirely.

questions.q: Which of the following is true about what Numba's nopython mode can compile?
options: It can compile arbitrary Python objects and any third-party library call
It only understands a limited subset: NumPy arrays, numeric scalars, basic control flow, and an allow-listed set of NumPy functions -- not arbitrary objects or most of the standard library
It can compile pandas DataFrame methods natively but not NumPy arrays
It requires all code to be rewritten in Cython syntax first
questions.explain: Nopython mode is restricted to a numeric subset of Python -- arrays, scalars, basic control flow, and specific supported functions -- which is why the numeric core of a computation is typically pulled into a small @njit function.

questions.q: In the real benchmark, what happened when `parallel=True` and `prange` were added to the n=2000 pairwise example?
options: It was dramatically faster than the single-threaded `@njit` version
It was roughly the same speed as, or slightly slower than, the single-threaded `@njit` version, because thread overhead offset the gain at that workload size
It failed to compile
It produced a different, incorrect result
questions.explain: The measured numbers showed the parallel version (25.0 ms) was not faster than the plain @njit version (23.2 ms) on this 4-core machine at this workload size -- parallel=True adds overhead that only pays off with a large enough per-core workload.

questions.q: What does `fastmath=True` trade away in exchange for potential speed?
options: Memory safety
Strict IEEE-754 floating-point rules, allowing reordering that may not be bit-for-bit identical to the unrelaxed result
The ability to use NumPy arrays
Thread safety
questions.explain: fastmath relaxes strict IEEE-754 floating-point semantics to allow faster operation reordering, at the cost of exact bit-for-bit reproducibility -- usually acceptable for aggregate numerical work but worth knowing about.
